summary: Number 29 of South Korean Interim Government Activities, prepared by the National Economic Board for USAMGIK, covers February 1948. Cold-war tension dominates: leftist sabotage and strikes from 7 February, the UN Interim Committee's 27 February decision to observe elections in South Korea alone, the split between Rhee, Kim Koo and Kimm Kiu-sic, and the walkout of Speaker Kimm and 30 legislators that crippled the Interim Legislative Assembly. The report also records completion of rice collection at 97.6 per cent of quota, continued industrial shortages of bituminous coal, power and parts, record revenues exceeding expenditures for the first time since liberation, price indexes still rising, vested property disposal and land reform, police and civil-liberties reforms ahead of the May elections, and a 58 per cent rise in northern refugees. Detailed statistical tables on population, prices, production, trade, finance and labor, plus feature studies on the Korean National Youth, women and the flag, make it a rich source for historians of the occupation.
highlights: The UN Interim Committee decided on 27 February, 31 to 2, to observe elections in South Korea alone, overshadowing every other development of the month.
Leftists began a revolt on 7 February; sabotage and riots brought 1,489 arrests in 7-12 February, with 6 police and 29 rioters killed, but no nation-wide general strike developed.
Speaker Kimm Kiu-sic and 30 legislators walked out of KILA over the rightists' Urgent Proposal to the UN, which passed amended 40 to 0 on 23 February and halted the Assembly.
Rice collection ended 15 February with 97.6 per cent of quota (754,579 metric tons) collected, though 225,000 tons of cereal imports are projected as needed in 1948/49.
For the first time since liberation, February revenue deposits exceeded withdrawals, by a net 386 million won, while Bank of Chosun note circulation fell 722 million won.
Refugee inflow from north of the 38th parallel rose 58 per cent over January, with 4,074 processed in February.
The Seoul retail price index reached 2,310, rising for a ninth straight month, while bituminous coal imports from Japan hit a record 83,330 tons, with 50,000 extra tons allotted for power.

Police administrative authority was placed under provincial governors, except on organization, administration, finances and personnel, as a safeguard against a police state, alongside new civil-liberties recommendations.

sections.title: Front matter
sections.summary: Cover of No. 29 (February 1948), prepared by the National Economic Board for USAMGIK, Google scan pages and printed contents (pp. i-v) listing Parts I-VI.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.summary: Reviews February 1948 under cold-war tension: leftist revolt and sabotage from 7 February, the UN Interim Committee's 27 February decision on South-only elections, and Speaker Kimm Kiu-sic's walkout with 30 legislators from KILA.

sections.title: Part I: Basic Aspects
sections.summary: Covers population and foreign affairs, where refugees from the North rose 58 per cent, and vested property, where sales stayed slow and leasing (299 plants) was tried.

sections.title: Section 1: Population and Foreign Affairs
sections.summary: Refugees from the North rose 58 per cent over January (4,074 processed). The 1947 Seoul census counted 779,890 adults. Also Koreans in Manchuria (about 800,000), Osaka Korean schools and 192 illegal entrants.

sections.title: Section 2: Vested Property
sections.summary: Vested property sales stalled for lack of reputable Korean buyers, so leasing (299 plants) and reorganization (409 companies examined) were tried; February sales totaled 35 for 4,600,800 won, with 423 audits.

sections.title: Part II: Production and Supply
sections.summary: Covers food, agriculture, prices, industry, mining, allocation, trade and labor: rice collection reached 97.6 per cent of quota, retail prices rose a ninth month, coal and power stayed short, and unions reported 84,363 members.

sections.title: Section 1: Food Supply
sections.summary: The 1947/48 rice collection ended 15 February at 97.6 per cent of quota (754,579 metric tons); only Cholla-pukto fell well short. Grain imports were 4,102 tons, and 225,000 tons of cereal imports are projected for 1948/49.

sections.title: Section 2: Agriculture, Forestry and Fisheries
sections.summary: Covers FAO 1950 census planning, 123 crop-reporting employees trained, and the New Korea Company's 324,604 chungbo, to be sold at three times annual crop value over 15 years. Kyonggi-do 4-H clubs grew to 1,072.

sections.title: Section 3: Prices
sections.summary: Seoul retail prices rose a ninth straight month, the index reaching 2,310, nearly four per cent above January. The wholesale index fell to 6,910, over six per cent below January's record. Rice control price steady since November 1945.

sections.title: Section 4: Industrial Production
sections.summary: Industrial output stayed low, with data mostly for January. Shortages of wheat, pulp, pitch, coal and power hit flour, paper, briquettes and cement; Puksan paper mill resumed after 10 months, and government salterns were idle.

sections.title: Section 5: Mining and Minerals
sections.summary: January anthracite output reached 41,357 metric tons, 32 per cent above December. Bituminous imports from Japan hit a record 83,330 tons in February, with 50,000 extra tons allotted for power; pitch stayed scarce.

sections.title: Section 6: Allocations and Distribution
sections.summary: The new Consumer Goods Allocation Board and National Consumer Goods Office only organized in February. About 22,000,000 won of Civil Service Relief Committee goods were inventoried; 223,000,000 won of year-end bonus goods were distributed.

sections.title: Section 7: Imports and Exports
sections.summary: Private trade estimates for February were imports of 260 million won against exports of 421 million. New Trustee Shipment and export-loan rules were issued; government cargoes included laver exports and coal, fertilizer, rice and salt imports.

sections.title: Section 8: Labor
sections.summary: A seamen's bargaining election was set for 5-7 March in six ports, and Pungkuk Flour Mills agreed to pay back wages. Unions reported 84,363 members; Seoul Electric Company's union contract was extended.

sections.title: Part III: Public Services
sections.summary: Covers transportation, communications, utilities and public works: rail fares rose 25 to 50 per cent, sabotage damaged 52 locomotives, power delivered was 72,000,000 KWH, and highway man-days reached 171,451.

sections.title: Section 1: Transportation
sections.summary: New rail, marine and highway rates took effect, rail fares rising 25 per cent (first and second class) and 50 per cent (third). Sabotage from 7 February damaged 52 locomotives and ended night passenger trains.

sections.title: Section 2: Communications
sections.summary: About 7,500 would-be telephone subscribers went unserved despite marked growth in 1947. January revenue fell from December, expenditures rose 1,000,000 won, an emergency transmitter was installed and 20,000 radios were repaired.

sections.title: Section 3: Public Utilities
sections.summary: Power delivered to distributors in February was 72,000,000 KWH, of which 24,000,000 were produced in South Korea. The Emergency Power Board extended the curfew from 2200 to 2300; Seoul tram fares rose to five won from 5 March.

sections.title: Section 4: Public Works
sections.summary: Mild weather let road and bridge repairs begin early; highway man-days reached 171,451. Some 236,753,123.85 won was spent on the Seoul-Pusan road, 50,000,000 won of flood funds allocated, and 149 fires caused 219,143,550 won loss.

sections.title: Part IV: Finance
sections.summary: Covers government finance, where revenue deposits exceeded withdrawals for the first time and notes outstanding fell 722 million won, and non-government finance, where January deposits rose 6,882 million won to 52,208 million.

sections.title: Section 1: Government Finance
sections.summary: Bank of Chosun notes fell 722 million won, and revenue deposits exceeded withdrawals by a net 386 million won for the first time. The Military Governor ordered a balanced 1948/49 budget of about 22,000 million won.

sections.title: Section 2: Non-Government Finance
sections.summary: January data only: total deposits rose 6,882 million won, over 15 per cent, to 52,208 million, and cash balances rose over 614 million. Loans fell 1,062 million won; the Foreign Exchange Bank made its first trade loan.

sections.title: Part V: Government and Politics
sections.summary: Covers administration, the legislature, politics, law, police and interzone affairs: the Urgent Proposal split KILA, the UN Interim Committee approved South Korean elections 31 to 2, and the 7-12 February riots brought 1,489 arrests.

sections.title: Section 1: Administration
sections.summary: Maj.-Gen. Helmick was in Washington 19 January to 4 February to justify 1948/49 GARIOA and rehabilitation funds. Silk was decontrolled, coal prices raised, and a reorganization plan would cut 40 per cent of bureaus.

sections.title: Section 2: Korean Interim Legislative Assembly
sections.summary: KILA approved the 1947 budget 38 to one on 2 February. The rightists' Urgent Proposal asking the UN Commission for a South Korean election passed amended 40 to 0 on 23 February; Speaker Kimm Kiu-sic and Vice-Speaker Choe Tong-O resigned.

sections.title: Section 3: Political Developments
sections.summary: Rhee Syngman's rightists favored a separate South Korean election, while Kimm Kiu-sic and Kim Koo wanted a North-South leaders' conference. The three leaders met 10 February; the UN Interim Committee approved a South Korean election 31 to 2 on 27 February.

sections.title: Section 4: Legal Affairs
sections.summary: The Department of Justice published an order barring separate Sam Il Day demonstrations and issued opinions on overtime pay and vested property. 191 guards graduated, and Korean courts admitted five northern lawyers.

sections.title: Section 5: National Police
sections.summary: Police Department civil-liberties recommendations included release after three days without charge. The 7-12 February strike and riot wave brought 1,489 arrests, with 6 police and 29 rioters killed; provincial police chiefs answer to governors.

sections.title: Section 6: Interzone Activities
sections.summary: More than 45,000 pieces of mail crossed the 38th parallel at Tosong. Radio Pyongyang covered the 8 February inauguration of the Korean People's Army; the draft North Korean constitution (102 articles) was broadcast 16 February.

sections.title: Part VI: Social
sections.summary: Covers health, education, culture, press, youth and women: 62,198 of 173,305 deaths were children under five, middle school tuition rises to 1,800 won, and Korean National Youth reached 519,938 members.

sections.title: Section 1: Public Health and Welfare
sections.summary: A study found 62,198 of 173,305 deaths in April-December 1946 were children under five, about 40 per cent preventable with penicillin or sulfonamides. Typhus, typhoid and diphtheria led; prostitution was banned 14 February.

sections.title: Section 2: Education
sections.summary: Provincial education directors met 18-19 February. Middle school tuition rises from 600 to 1,800 won from 1 April and elementary tuition is abolished; 500,000 surplus textbooks were obtained and 182 English teachers completed a course.

sections.title: Section 3: Culture
sections.summary: An essay explains the Tai Guk symbol on the Korean flag; year 4281 was celebrated 10 February. Kim Che-won and Kim Won-yong won Rockefeller fellowships; HLKA marked its 21st anniversary and the first New Korean Dictionary volume appeared.

sections.title: Section 4: Press and Public Opinion
sections.summary: Press centered on the UN Temporary Commission, with calls for unity after Gandhi's murder. Papers covered the 7-10 February strikes (8,479 arrests by 26 February) and a 7,000,000 won bribery scandal.

sections.title: Section 5: Korean National Youth, Inc.
sections.summary: The 22-23 February council of 227 delegates re-elected Lee Bum-suk as president. Membership reached 519,938 against a 600,000 goal after leftist infiltration during the 7 February riots was blocked.

sections.title: Section 6: Women's Activities
sections.summary: Korean women served as UN Commission hostesses. The Women's Bureau (Director Koh Whang-kyung, founded September 1946) published "New Homemaking" and moved to Hokuksa Temple 27 February; the Altrusa Club awarded a nursing fellowship.

sections.title: Back matter
sections.summary: Blank Google-digitized pages, a back-cover image, a library date-due slip (stamped June 2010) and a final page of meaningless OCR symbols.
